w: Order fries at Termini station and eat them beside a slab of wall Rome built after the Gauls sacked the city in 390 BC. The Servian Wall turns up in odd corners across the capital, but nowhere quite so bluntly as behind glass in a fast-food dining room, ancient stone unbothered by the golden arches.
s: 2,500-year-old city wall, right behind the fry station
_facts: a preserved section of the 4th-century BC Servian Wall sits inside a McDonald's dining area near Roma Termini station
the McDonald's is at Via Giovanni Giolitti 65, on the south side of Termini
the wall dates to the rebuilding of Rome's defences after the Gallic sack of the city around 390 BC
the largest surviving stretch of the same wall stands just outside the station

w: A circus impresario opened Rome's wax museum in 1958 after touring the great collections of Europe, and it has been quietly outliving fashion ever since. Popes, actors and ancient Romans stand shoulder to shoulder near Palazzo Colonna, and the workshop door is left open so visitors can watch the figures get made.
s: popes and gladiators in wax, running since 1958
_facts: founded in 1958 by circus entrepreneur Fernando Canini after he toured Europe's major wax museums
moved to its current site near Piazza dei Santi Apostoli / Palazzo Colonna around 1969-70
billed as the third-largest wax collection in Europe, with themed rooms on popes, actors, painters and ancient Rome
lets visitors see into the workshop where the wax figures are made and restored

w: Sixty-three seats in a green chalet tucked into Villa Borghese make this the smallest cinema in the world, Guinness-certified. It opened in 1934 as Cinema Topolino until Disney's lawyers objected to the borrowed Mickey Mouse name, and it still screens matinees for kids and arthouse films for grown-ups.
_facts: 63-seat cinema inside Villa Borghese park, recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's smallest cinema
opened in 1934 by Alfredo Annibali, originally named Cinema Topolino ('Mickey Mouse') after the Disney character
renamed Cinema dei Piccoli after Disney objected to the unauthorised name
still screens daytime children's films and evening original-language arthouse films

w: Four hundred and twenty-six Commonwealth graves sit against the Aurelian Walls a few steps from the Pyramid of Cestius, buried here after Rome's liberation in June 1944. Traffic on Piazzale Ostiense roars nearby, but step through the gate and it drops to almost nothing. One of the quietest corners in the city.
s: 426 commonwealth graves, silent behind the aurelian wall
_facts: Commonwealth War Graves Commission cemetery on Via Nicola Zabaglia, designed by Louis de Soissons
contains 426 Commonwealth burials from the Second World War
lies alongside the ancient Aurelian Walls, adjoining the Protestant Cemetery near the Pyramid of Cestius
became a burial ground for occupying Allied troops after the German withdrawal from Rome in June 1944

w: Three Roman temples, to Janus, Juno Sospita and Hope, got swallowed whole by a medieval church built directly on top of them. Their columns still poke through the walls like bones through skin, and stairs beneath the altar lead down to the old temple floors. The building once served as a prison, hence the name.
s: three roman temples wearing a church as a disguise
_facts: the church stands on the site of the ancient Forum Holitorium, over three Republican-era Roman temples
columns from the Temple of Janus, Temple of Juno Sospita and Temple of Spes (Hope) are incorporated into the church's walls and facade
underground stairs lead to a crypt at the level of the old temple foundations
the site was used as a medieval prison ('carcere'), giving the church its name

n: Antica Spezieria di Santa Maria della Scala
w: Carmelite friars ran the oldest pharmacy in Rome from this frescoed room in Trastevere, mixing remedies for cardinals and popes until it closed in 1954. The ceiling still carries a coat of arms and portraits of Hippocrates and Galen, while the wooden cabinets and copper stills sit where the friars left them.
s: the popes' pharmacy, frescoed ceiling and all
_facts: founded in the 16th century by Discalced Carmelite friars above the church of Santa Maria della Scala in Trastevere
operated as a working pharmacy until 1954, nicknamed the 'pharmacy of the popes' for its clientele of cardinals and pontiffs
ceiling frescoed with the Carmelite coat of arms and portraits of physicians including Hippocrates and Galen
still holds original 18th-century wooden cabinets, majolica jars and distillation stills

w: Rome's municipal rose garden blooms on ground that was the city's Jewish cemetery for nearly three centuries, until burials moved to Verano in 1934. In tribute, the paths were laid out in the shape of a menorah, and a plaque at the gate remembers what came before the eleven hundred rose varieties now growing there.
s: a rose garden laid out in the shape of a menorah
_facts: municipal rose garden on the eastern slope of the Aventine Hill, at Via di Valle Murcia 6
the site served as Rome's Jewish cemetery from the mid-17th century until 1934, when burials moved to Verano
the garden's paths are arranged in the shape of a menorah in tribute to that history
holds around 1,100 rose varieties from around the world
